newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia govt rejects calls for Colston inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Australia govt rejects calls for Colston inquiry.

text.p: The Australian government on Monday again rejected calls for a parliamentary inquiry into allegations that key independent senator Mal Colston had lied to parliament.
Government leader in the upper house of parliament, Robert Hill, said such an inquiry was likely to prejudice a police investigation into linked claims surrounding Colston.
"That may well prejudice the police inquiry or matters that could subsequently flow from that inquiry," Hill told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
"Therefore, for the (upper house) Senate to take that action because it feels that it needs to do something internally would be reckless and irresponsible," he said.
On Sunday, the Clerk of the Senate, Harry Evans, recommended that the upper house hold an inquiry into the Colston claims even if the probe caused "some inconvenience" to the police.
But the government's chief general counsel, Henry Burmester, warned that an inquiry could prevent material from being used in any court action stemming from the criminal investigation.

Police are investigating Colston, an independent who defected from the Labor opposition in August last year and whose vote is crucial to the passage of government legislation, over alleged false expense claims. Colston denies any wrongdoing.

The proposed Senate inquiry would centre on Colston's statement to parliament that unjustified expense claims were the result of "sloppy book-keeping" on the part of former office manager Christine Smith.
Colston himself last month paid back 43 nights of overclaimed travel allowances, but blamed Smith for the errors.
But earlier this month Smith recanted her statement that she was responsible for the claims, prompting the government to ask police to include the matter in their investigations.
"The problem is that it all arises out of the same set of facts," Hill said.
"That's why it's been my concern all along that a Senate inquiry might prejudice the police investigation and I therefore thought that it was unwise that it should go ahead," he said.
"Harry Evans says that he feels that the issues could be kept distinct, but I very much doubt that."
Colston was released from a Brisbane hospital last week after suffering an unspecified medical condition. He is currently convalescing at an undisclosed location.
